source.title: MicroEdit: Neuron-level Knowledge Disentanglement and Localization in Lifelong Model Editing
source.authors: Shiqi Wang; Qi Wang; Run-Liang Niu; He Kong; Yi Chang

record.file_problem: None apparent; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses pretrained SAEs as a tool for neuron-level knowledge editing and reports editing performance. It does not test superposition geometry, capacity competition, or whether SAE features are canonical units. Its activation analyses are related but do not measure the geometrical claims in the listed versions.
record.gate_note: Figure 1 reports neuron activation rates, output changes after masking, activation-strategy comparisons, and activation overlap across knowledge statements. These findings are recorded as related results under fits_no_version because they do not measure the feature geometry or capacity accounts named by the versions. Editing benchmark results and ablations are omitted: they report MicroEdit's editing performance, not the claim's feature geometry or SAE feature recovery. The paper cites Toy Models of Superposition but does not reproduce its method.
record.test_reason: MicroEdit uses pretrained SAEs (EleutherAI LLaMA-3-8B, SAE Lens Mistral-7B) as an editing tool and reports editing performance (Tables 1-6). Its Section 2 activation analyses (Figure 1) measure neuron activation sparsity and activation overlap between knowledge statements. They do not test toy-model geometry, capacity competition, other causes of polysemanticity, SAE feature recovery or canonicity, or feature dimensionality. The polysemanticity of neurons is cited from Elhage et al. and Bricken et al. and assumed, not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that edit overshooting and knowledge entanglement, which they attribute to neuron polysemanticity, limit lifelong editing. They conclude that Top-k SAE activation with decoder-only updates and an ARD-based switch reduces interference and outperforms baselines on ZsRE and SelfCheckGPT. The polysemanticity attribution is asserted from prior work and a small 10-statement overlap analysis, not tested.
record.recipe_differences: The study applies pretrained SAEs to LLM knowledge editing, freezing the base model and SAE encoder and updating the SAE decoder. It does not reproduce the original toy-model setup or its geometry measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Editing performance changes with layer choice, Top-k size, and ARD threshold; the paper reports best performance at k = 192 for the LLaMA SAE and at ARD threshold 0.55 in the reported ZsRE threshold study.

fits_no_version.finding: Neuron activation is sparse in early and middle layers and rises in deeper layers. Keeping the top 60% of activated neurons preserves outputs, and highly activated neurons are needed for target knowledge (Figure 1a-c; model not stated).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LLM outputs for factual prompts depend on a subset of highly activated neurons, with activation density increasing by depth.

fits_no_version.finding: Semantically unrelated knowledge statements share up to 18% of activated neurons (10 statements, Figure 1e-f).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unrelated knowledge statements share activated neurons in LLM layers, which the authors interpret as polysemanticity.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (2025)
record.problems: The Figure 1 analysis uses only 10 randomly selected knowledge statements for the overlap examples. Numerical values for the plotted activation analyses are not given in the text, and no uncertainty estimates are reported. The paper does not directly measure feature directions or superposition geometry.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 1-6 and the associated editing ablations, layer tests, and threshold tests report knowledge-editing performance rather than feature geometry, capacity competition, or SAE feature recovery; excluded under the gate rule.

untested.parts: No toy model, no geometry, and no sparsity-dependent transition.
Does not test whether neuron sharing arises from capacity competition or from feature importance.
Does not test alternative causes of polysemanticity.

Figure 1(e-f) shows activated-neuron overlap between unrelated statements (up to 18%, 10 statements). It does not show features distributed across neurons, and it does not evaluate whether SAEs recover sparse features; SAEs are used only as an editing substrate.
No test of SAE feature completeness, stability or canonicity. The Top-k study (Figure 4) measures editing performance, not feature quality.

record.verdict_notes: The Figure 1 model is unstated; it is likely LLaMA-3-8B, but the text does not confirm this. The record's exclusion of the editing tables is appropriate: they compare the study's own method with baselines. The paper cites the original source (Elhage et al. 2022) only as background.

versions.untested_parts: No toy-network experiment or test of overlapping, nearly orthogonal directions, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular geometry.
Does not test whether polysemanticity results from capacity competition, or whether feature importance determines dedicated versus shared dimensions.
Does not test alternative causes of polysemanticity or whether polysemantic neurons are evidence for superposition.
Uses pretrained SAEs but does not assess whether their features recover the model's features, or whether model features are distributed across neurons.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
Does not measure whether represented features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional.
